summary: Describes the Internet X.509 PKI Certificate Management Protocol, with messages for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates. It supports online exchanges between a certification authority and a client. It is a standards-track document, replaced by RFC 9810.

eli5.summary: Certificates are digital ID cards. This memo defines the messages used to ask for, renew and cancel those ID cards from the issuer.

questions: what is the certificate management protocol
how does cmp prove possession of a private key
what does a registration authority do
subtitle: The messages a certificate authority and its clients use to request, renew, update and revoke X.509 certificates online.

tldr.problem: A public key infrastructure needs a standard way for end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities to create and manage X.509v3 certificates, instead of every product inventing its own exchange.
tldr.mechanism: CMP defines a PKIMessage with a header, a body chosen from a list of message types, optional protection and optional extra certificates, plus the exchanges for registration, key update, recovery, revocation and cross-certification.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4210 obsoleted RFC 2510 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9810, so new work should follow the newer specification.

today: RFC 4210 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9810. It was updated by RFC 6712, RFC 9480 and RFC 9481, and it obsoleted RFC 2510.

sections.title: Introduction and What Changed
sections.content:
RFC 4210 describes the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) of the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). It defines protocol messages for creating and managing X.509v3 certificates, including on-line exchanges between a Certification Authority (CA) and a client system.

It obsoletes RFC 2510. The main differences are that the message profiles are split into a required appendix and an optional appendix, the confirmation mechanism changed substantially, and a new polling mechanism replaces the old polling at the transport level. Transport is now handled in a separate document, and a new implicit confirmation method reduces the number of messages in a transaction.
sections.eli5: This document is a rulebook for the paperwork of digital ID cards. The new version simplified some steps and moved the mailing details to another document.

sections.title: The PKI Management Model
sections.content:
Three kinds of party take part. The end entity is whoever the certificate is issued to, and it can be a person or an application. The certification authority issues the certificates. A registration authority (RA) is an optional component that may handle things like personal authentication, token distribution, revocation reporting, name assignment and key generation. When no RA is present, the CA is assumed to do the RA's work, so the protocol looks the same from the end entity's side.

A root CA is one that an end entity trusts directly, learned through some out-of-band step. Every end entity needs secure local access to its own name and private key, the name of a directly trusted CA and that CA's public key. The RFC calls this the Personal Security Environment.

The operations covered include CA establishment, end entity initialization, initial registration and certification, key pair update, certificate update, CA key pair update, cross-certification, certificate and CRL publication, key pair recovery and revocation requests. The document notes that on-line protocols are not the only way to do any of this, and off-line methods are also allowed.

Final authority rests with the CA. A certificate it issues may differ from what was requested, for example with a shorter validity period, and every party must be able to cope with that.
sections.eli5: There is the person who wants an ID card, the office that makes it, and sometimes a helper desk that checks who you are first. If there is no helper desk, the office does that job too.

sections.title: The PKIMessage Structure
sections.content:
Every CMP message is a PKIMessage with four parts: a header, a body, optional protection and optional extraCerts. The header carries the version (pvno, fixed at 2 for this specification), the sender and recipient, and fields for protection, transaction tracking and free text. The extraCerts field lets a CA or RA hand over certificates the recipient may need to verify a new certificate.

The transactionID ties messages of one transaction together. Clients are RECOMMENDED to fill it with 128 bits of random data. The senderNonce and recipNonce guard against replay: the recipient copies the sender's nonce from the previous message. If a transaction ID is already in use, the server MUST answer with an error whose failure information is transactionIdInUse.

The body is a choice among message types such as ir (initialization request), cr (certification request), kur (key update request), krr (key recovery request), rr (revocation request), ccr (cross-certification request), certConf, pollReq and error, with matching responses and announcements. Responses carry a status such as accepted, grantedWithMods, rejection or waiting, and failures can add details like badPOP or badMessageCheck.

Two optional header extensions help with confirmation. ImplicitConfirm lets the end entity say it will not send a certificate confirmation, and if the CA agrees it echoes the extension. ConfirmWaitTime tells the end entity how long the CA will wait for confirmation before revoking the certificate and deleting the transaction.
sections.eli5: Every message is an envelope with an address label, a letter, and an optional seal. The label has a random number so replies match the right conversation and old letters cannot be replayed.

sections.title: Protecting Messages and Proving Key Possession
sections.content:
The protection field is computed over the DER encoding of the header and body, in one of three ways. With shared secret information it holds a MAC, using id-PasswordBasedMac, which repeatedly applies a one-way function to the salted secret. With Diffie-Hellman key pairs it holds a MAC keyed from the DH result (id-DHBasedMac). With a signature the sender signs the message. An RA can forward an end entity's message by nesting it inside a new message with its own protection, and may batch several requests of the same type.

CAs and RAs MUST enforce proof of possession (POP): the requester must show it can use the private key matching the public key being certified, because many operational protocols do not check that binding. For signature keys the end entity signs a value. For encryption keys it can hand over the private key, or decrypt a value. The RFC encourages the indirect method, where the certificate is issued encrypted and decrypting it is shown in the confirmation message, since it needs no extra messages. For key agreement keys a shared secret is established.

For initial registration, the one scheme all implementations MUST support is the basic authenticated scheme: the end entity generates its keys, protects the request with an out-of-band initial authentication key, and the exchange ends with a confirmation message. If confirmation verification fails, the RA or CA MUST revoke the newly issued certificate if it was published.
sections.eli5: To get an ID card you must show you really own the secret key it is for, the way you would show you can open a lock. Messages are also sealed so nobody can change them on the way.

sections.title: Mandatory Functions, Polling and Version Negotiation
sections.content:
Section 6 lists functions all end entity and CA or RA implementations MUST provide, including root CA initialization and key update, subordinate CA initialization, CRL production, PKI information requests, cross-certification, end entity initialization, certificate requests and key update. The root CA key update works by having the CA protect its new public key with its old private key and vice versa, which is why four certificates (OldWithOld, OldWithNew, NewWithOld and NewWithNew) are involved.

When a CA cannot answer at once, for instance because manual approval is needed, it returns the waiting status. The client then sends a pollReq, and the CA returns either the finished response or a pollRep with a checkAfter time in seconds. The client waits at least that long before polling again.

Version negotiation is simple. A client sends the highest version both sides support, or its own highest if it does not know. A server replies with the same version, or with an error marked unsupportedVersion if it does not support the one received. Servers MAY fall back to RFC 2510 behavior (version cmp1999).
sections.eli5: If the office cannot make your card right away, it says to come back later. You check again after the time they gave you, until it is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls out three risks. First, proving possession of a decryption key means decrypting something, and that could be abused if a key holder can be fooled into decrypting an arbitrary challenge and returning the plaintext, so implementations should be careful about revealing recovered plaintext. Second, proving possession by handing over the private key carries risk unless the CA or RA can be trusted, so the user should explicitly agree first.

Third, a malicious end entity could choose Diffie-Hellman parameters that leak bits of the CA's DH private key during key archival or recovery (a small subgroup attack). The RECOMMENDED defense is for the CA to generate a fresh DH key pair for each end entity it deals with.
sections.eli5: Do not let anyone trick you into unlocking random boxes for them, be careful before giving a copy of your secret key to someone, and use a fresh lock each time.
